issues.title: Add newer hmacs to PBKDF2-PRFs
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
In [RFC 6402](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6402#appendix-A.2),  defines kda-PBKDF2 for use with KeyDevAlgs, which is used in the PopLinkWitnessV2 control.  If you look at kda-PBKDF2, which is imported from [RFC 5911](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5911#section-3) only alg-hMAC-SHA1 is included. Obviously, we need to add additional algorithms there, so we need to update PBKDF2-PRFs to include additional algorithms.  We are proposing adding the following algorithms:

    alg-hMAC-SHA224
    alg-hMAC-SHA256
    alg-hMAC-SHA384
    alg-hMAC-SHA512
    alg-hMAC-SHA512-224
    alg-hMAC-SHA512-256

This requires a new module and probably adding "updates 5911" to the header.

issues.title: Suggestions for 6.7.  Encrypted and Decrypted POP Controls
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
In 6.7, "the hash of" has been inserted in

         3.  Client decrypts the POP challenge using the private key that corresponds to the 
              presented public key and sends the hash of the plaintext back to the server.    

This is certainly an improvement over the original sentence, but still not really correct.
Should better be, e.g., 

         3.  Client decrypts the POP challenge using the private key that corresponds to the 
              presented public key and uses it for computing a keyed hash value sent back to the server.    

While being at this, I suggest making also 

    The second deals with the decrypted challenge sent from the client to the server in Step 3.

more precise/correct, e.g., adapting it to

    The second deals with the value derived from the decrypted challenge sent by the client to the server in Step 3.

issues.title: B.3 - POP Round Trip
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
In B.3, the statement 

   The fact that a second round-trip is required is implicit rather than
   explicit.  The server determines this based on the fact that no other
   POP exists for the certification request.
appears wrong because the Message #1 contains the "keyEncipherment" choice with "subsequentMessage" in the "popo" field:

               popo
                 keyEncipherment
                   subsequentMessage
which already indicates the need for some form of encrypted POP. So please correct this statement or explain suitably.

issues.title: B.3 - Signature Certificate
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
Regarding the sentence: 

 For simplicity, it is assumed that the certification requester already has a signing-only certificate.

Any signing-capable cert/key, not just a signing-only cert, will work for the signature-based authentication of the CMC requests.
What if the requester or server has just a KEM certificate and thus cannot sign messages for their authentication?

issues.title: B.3 / B.4 - Fix Requests
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
At least in B.3 and B.4, the syntax and descriptions of the requests (which are partly repeated in the responses) is sketchy.
Most of this has been simply taken over from RFC 5262, which has mostly the same deficiencies.
For instance, in

           reqSequence
             certRequest
               certReqId = 201
               certTemplate
                 subject = <My DN from my signing cert>
                 publicKey = My Public Key
                 extensions
                   {id-ce-keyUsage, keyEncipherment}
                   {id-ce-subjectPublicKeyIdentifier, 1000}
               popo
                 keyEncipherment
                   subsequentMessage
in "subject = <My DN from my signing cert>" (used several times), better leave out "from my signing cert" 
because in general the new cert will have a different subject than the one used to authenticate the request.
the field name "crm" (of type CertReqMsg) is missing between reqSequence and certRequest, and the name "certRequest" is wrong - it should read "certReq"
the "popo" field should not be at same level as "certTemplate", as it is a direct sub-field of "crm", not of certReq
the subsequentMessage is missing its integer value, which in this case must be 1 (for challengeResp, see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4211.html#section-4.2)

issues.title: B.3 / B.4 - Fix Response # 1
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
In the Response #1 (in both B.3 and B.4), 

In recipientInfos.riid.issuerSerialNumber, "riid" is wrong and should read "rid".
Please mention in B.3 and B.4 that the 'y' in
		eContent = <Encrypted value of 'y'>
	and 
		witness <hashed value of 'y'>
	is the POP Proof Value as defined at the end of section 6.7.

Some hints on how to fill in the non-trivial "cms" field of type EnvelopedData may be helpful.
The "Other certificates (optional)" may be confusing - please mention that these are only related to the signature of the response and do not already include the requested certificate, will be included only in the final response.
BTW, I doubt that it was a good design decision that the EncryptedPOP structure must repeat the whole request  -
the advantage mentioned in section 6.7 that the client does not strictly need to remember the request data comes with some downsides:
the client either still needs keep a copy in order to check consistency with its request or needs to trust in the server not having altered it,
and the larger KEM public keys may need to become in future, the bigger the waste. 
Would have been good to allow giving instead just the certReqId.

issues.title: 5273: binary requests
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
From review:

In §4 (File-Based Protocol) there's a line about "When files are used to
transport binary, Full PKI Request or Full PKI Response messages" and a table
that lists four message types.  I'm not sure I understand what the "binary"
maps to -- initially I thought that the comma was a typo and we're just
clarifying that the Full PKI Request/Response use binary encodings, but then I
started to wonder if "binary request or response" refers to the .p10 and .p7c
formats.  For what it's worth, "binary" only appears in RFC 5727 in comments
describing what's in the example message exchange, so I'm inclined to believe
that "binary reqest/response" is not currently a CMC term of art.
(I also kind of expect that the "simple" requests/responses, by nature of
their file type, can only contain a single request/response and so there's no
need to specifically state a requirement, which tends to support the theory
that the comma is a typo.)

issues.title: 5273: TCP pipelining
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
From review:

I think that it is probably not safe to attempt to "pipeline" requests over a
TCP connection (starting to send another request before the full response has
been received to the first request), but we only implicitly at best cover this
situation.  I'd suggest making a clear statement about whether or not the
client needs to wait for the full response before making another request on
the same connection.

issues.title: 5273: SecCons for EnvelopedData
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
From the review:

We have a nice note (§9) about using EnvelopedData to provide content
shrouding in cases where TLS cannot be used.  But this is the security
considerations section; we should talk about what the risks are and why one
might want to have some kind of content shrouding at all (whether via TLS or
EnvelopedData)!

It's also interesting to note that the phrasing is "EnvelopedData ... must be
used" (lowerase must), which leaves it unclear whether there's an analogous
requirement to use TLS when it's possible to use TLS.  Perhaps we're just
saying that EnvelopedData is the only way to get content shrouding when TLS is
not available, in which case we probably want to avoid a "must be used"
construction.

issues.title: Other use cases: security considerations
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
"In most circumstances, the use of HTTP over TLS [HTTP] provides any necessary
content protection from eavesdroppers."

"In most circumstances..:" - what would be an example of other cases? Is there
something the security considerations should include?

Also, this should say "the use of HTTPS" -- the important thing is the use of a
secure channel. For instance, HTTP/3 does not use TLS.

"Servers MUST use the 200 response code for successful responses."

I understand that this may be hard to change after the fact, but it's not clear

comments.body: I can't imagine this was anything other than an oversight and it should just be 2XX as opposed to 200.

issues.title: client requests
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
"Clients MAY attempt to send HTTP requests using TLS 1.2 [TLS] or later,
although servers are not required to support TLS. If TLS is supported by an
implementation, then the implementation MUST folow the recommendations in
[BCP195]."

This sounds both severely outdated and over-specified. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
define their requirements for HTTPS connections already. In particular, HTTP/3
does not use TCP at all.

issues.title: Edit sentence for client auth
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
"Servers MUST NOT assume client support for any type of HTTP authentication
such as cookies, Basic authentication, or Digest authentication."

Maybe: "Clients are not required to support any kind of HTTP authentication
([HTTP], Section 11) nor Cookies ([RFC6265]). Thus, servers can not rely on
these features to be available."

issues.title: Support chunked transfer encoding
issues.author: mandelj7
issues.body:
"Clients and servers are expected to follow the other rules and restrictions in
[HTTP]. Note that some of those rules are for HTTP methods other than POST;
clearly, only the rules that apply to POST are relevant for this specification."

Hm, not really. For instance, servers have to support GET and HEAD (that's a
basic HTTP requirement), clients need to properly process 1xx responses. Is
support for chunked transfer encoding required? (see RFC 9112, Section 6.1)?
Are requests using chunked transfer encoding forbidden?

    about "a secure channel [...] constructed between the end-entity and the
    CA", and SMTP-over-TLS provides only hop-by-hop security at best (with only
    a weak guarantee that all hops are actually protected); this doesn't really
    qualify as a "secure channel" in the usual sense.
    In order to approximate a secure channel we'd need to know (out of band)
    that the SMTP setup does reliably use TLS for all hops involved.

issues.title: 5273: Mail Text
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
@vdukhovni PTAL

Collecting some comments on an already merged PR:

https://github.com/lamps-wg/cmcbis/commit/45711d5749b1643581a1af1a4265eefad6ae7964#r169673166
https://github.com/lamps-wg/cmcbis/commit/45711d5749b1643581a1af1a4265eefad6ae7964#r169663242
https://github.com/lamps-wg/cmcbis/commit/fc32b30e6a61de4ae217f907e503ae30e68f689b#r169674615

We're interpreting some tea leaves here since neither Joe nor I was one of the original authors:

We believe this section was trying to tell implementers to make messages conform to what 1) should have been in [RFC 2986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2986.html) but ended up in in [s2.2 of RFC 5967](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5967.html#section-2.2) (application/pkcs10); 2) is in [s3.5.2 of RFC 8551](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8551.html#section-3.5.2) (application/pkcs7-mime); — and 3) not multipart.  I am hoping that if we reference massage in some references to RFCs 5967 and 8551 that would make it clearer?

On your other points:

- refer to correct parameter names: in light of above, we will attempt to clean up some of the language to make sure we refer to the correct parameters.
- file name requirement: pretty sure it was saying that you had to include some kind of value, i.e., you had to include the field and make sure it's not an empty string.
- As far as non-ASCII character support - you really got me!! Should this have been specified in the media type definitions? I'd personally lean toward prohibiting them.

We'll work on a PR.

comments.body:
Because this has been done for so long in many different ways, I am not sure what makes sense to say about this. In HTTP, I know that multipart/form-data is used by some/many. If we look at S/MIME, here's what I'm thinking:

- multipart/signed is used in S/MIME, but that's for detached signatures - and that doesn't make much sense with a CSR.
- multipart/alternative could be used, but are you really going to send a text and BER/DER version of the csr/cert?  Would send a "pretty print" part and then a BER part? I guess you could loosely think of the output of the OpenSSL `ca` command that concatenates both the "pretty print" and:
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
ASCII Cert goes here
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
as an input to something that is multipart/alternative. But, you don't need to send the pretty print part and the output of the command doesn't break it up that way - it's just one pem file.
- multipart/mixed could also be used maybe say if you were going to send a cover message that says "hi, attached is my CSR". But, I'm not sure we should really be getting into all the ways you could or could not put together an email with a CSR.

If you're the RA/CA and you're bundling of requests/responses, then you should/could be using the internal CMC fields to do the bundling so I'm not sure we need to go into all the ways you could do it via email.

Is there some other scenarios you're thinking about?

comments.author: vdukhovni
comments.body:
I seem to have completely failed to explain the issue. :-( :-(

It has NOTHING to do with the details of the `Content-Disposition:` header. It makes no difference whether that's "attachment" or "inline" unless a human is looking at with an interactive MUA, and not always even then.

The lack of specificity and clarity is about **WHERE** that `Content-Type:` or `Content-Disposition:` appears, is it the primary message header.  I rather expect the first alternative below, in which case the specified content (payload) is the entire message body, and "inline" vs. "attachment" is especially irrelevant, because primary message body is rarely presented as an "attachment", though automated tooling could arguably treat it differently.

The issue is whether the specification defines a complete RFC822  message (what I expect, but is not said), or some random nested MIME part, in which case how is that identified amongst all the other MIME part.  Is this a MIME sub-type specification, or a **message** format specification?

```email
Received: from ...
...
Received: from ...
From: ...
To: ...
Subject: ...
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: <as-specified>
Content-Disposition: <as-specified>

<specified content>
```
Or is the specified content in some multipart MIME structure:
```email
Received: from ...
From: ...
To: ...
Subject: ...
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=foo

--foo
Content-Type: whatever
Another-Header: ...

<a body part>

--foo
Content-Type: <as-specified>
Content-Disposition: <as-specified>

<specified content>
--foo
Content-Type: whatever
Another-Header: ...

<another (final) body part>

--foo--
```

LGTM, modulo one question:

* Is it, or should it be, made clear to the reader that the `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition` headers in question are present in the **primary** message header, not a nested MIME part header?

Or is it valid for the message to be a `multipart/alternative` or multipart/mixed`, ... with the required/described attachment somewhere in the resulting set of MIME multipart components?
